### 5.4.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty: Upholding Cognitive Integrity in the Algorithmic Era  

Confronted with the reality of cognitive disruption and algorithmic threats, the positive **Civil Law** doctrine—especially when drawn into Indonesian jurisdiction by reference to the tort provision in Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) and the doctrine of **Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent** in Articles 1320–1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) (*mistake* or *error* (*dwaling*), *fraud* or *deceit* (*bedrog*), and the doctrine of **Undue Influence** (*misbruik van omstandigheden*))—must be progressively and boldly reconstructed (Subekti, 2005; Mertokusumo, 2007). Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) unequivocally states that any act that violates the law and causes loss to another obliges the person who, by his fault, caused that loss to compensate the victim.  

The most crucial juridical question in the age of artificial intelligence is: before the law, who is the “person” that commits the fault when the harmful act is triggered by an autonomous machine’s output? The answer lies in the construction of corporate liability, wherein the developer corporation is positioned as a legal entity representing the collective shareholders, policy‑makers, and engineering designers who reap commercial profit from operating the system (Khanna, 2015; Kraakman, 2019).  

This doctrinal reconstruction demands the application of **strict liability** to AI developers in cases where severe psychological, physical, or financial harm arises from synthetic empathy manipulation or systematically misleading outputs (Shapo, 2012). Within this framework, the developer need not be shown to possess a personal *mens rea*; it suffices to demonstrate objectively that the product they release to the market, under normal operating conditions, creates a risk of harm that exceeds the socially unacceptable risk threshold (*socially unacceptable risk*) (Keeton et al., 1984).  

Furthermore, the limits of liability along the **digital supply chain**—from the core model **developer**, to the **cloud infrastructure provider**, to the downstream interface provider—must be delineated with surgical juridical precision (Susskind, 2020). A pure infrastructure provider that merely leases passive computing capacity may be afforded legal protection so long as it does not partake in model‑behavior design, whereas the primary developer who determines network architecture, training datasets, and safety protocols bears the principal legal burden.  

Ultimately, the entire edifice of civil liability doctrine converges on a single, lofty philosophical and constitutional aim: to protect, nurture, and reconstruct individual sovereignty amid an unrelenting storm of algorithmic manipulation (Froomkin, 2020). Individual sovereignty in the 21st century is no longer merely the classical right to be free from physical detention or coercion in the tangible world; it is a fundamental right to **Cognitive Liberty**—a new human right to think, feel, reflect, and make life decisions without being silently steered, manipulated, or exploited by attention‑harvesting machines designed solely for corporate profit accumulation (Sententia, 2004; Farahany, 2023). By enforcing a robust, uncompromising doctrine of *vicarious liability* in favor of substantive justice against AI developers, the global and national legal systems send a crystal‑clear message to the heart of the world’s technological power structures: no commercial innovation is valuable enough to be paid for with the destruction of human souls, and that above every line of the most intricate programming code stands the inviolable sovereignty of human dignity as the supreme law (*salus populi suprema lex*) (Cicero, 52 BC; Dworkin, 1986).
